stages.title: Protons, neutrons and electrons
stages.hook: Atoms of gold and atoms of oxygen are both made of the same three kinds of tiny parts. So what makes gold different from oxygen?
explain: An atom has a nucleus in the middle and electrons moving around it. The nucleus holds protons and neutrons. A proton has a positive charge, an electron has a negative charge, and a neutron has no charge.
A proton and a neutron have almost the same mass. An electron is about 1800 times lighter, so nearly all of an atom's mass is in the nucleus.
The number of protons decides which element an atom is. Every atom with 1 proton is hydrogen, with 6 protons is carbon, and with 8 protons is oxygen. This number is called the atomic number.
A normal atom is neutral: it has as many electrons as protons, so the positive and negative charges cancel.

example.q: A neutral atom of carbon has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. How many electrons does it have, and what is its mass number?
steps: Neutral means electrons = protons, so 6 electrons.

analogies.sport: Think of a team. The number of strikers decides the team's name; the other players do not change it.
analogies.home: A house's street number tells you which house it is. The proton number tells you which element it is.
analogies.music: Each element is like a note. The proton count sets the note.
analogies.city: The nucleus is the busy small centre, and electrons are the traffic moving around the edge.

stages.limits: Electrons do not orbit like planets. Modern physics describes them as clouds of probability. Protons and neutrons are made of smaller parts called quarks.

stages.title: Isotopes
stages.hook: Two carbon atoms sit side by side. One is a bit heavier. How can they both still be carbon?
explain: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same number of protons, so they are the same element.
We name an isotope by its mass number. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.
Isotopes behave almost the same in chemistry because they have the same number of electrons. But their nuclei can behave differently. Some are stable and some are unstable.
Unstable isotopes are radioactive. Carbon-14 is one of them. Scientists use it to estimate the age of once-living things such as old wood.

example.q: How many neutrons does carbon-14 have? (Carbon has 6 protons.)

panel.why: Stability depends on the proton to neutron balance.

teach.model: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons. They have the same number of protons, so they are the same element. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon, but carbon-14 has two more neutrons.

stages.title: Radioactivity
stages.hook: Some atoms change all by themselves without anyone touching them. Why would an atom do that?
explain: Some nuclei are unstable. They can change into a different, more stable nucleus. When they do, they give out energy as radiation. This is called radioactive decay.
Decay happens randomly. We cannot say when one particular atom will decay, but in a big group we can predict how many will decay in a given time.
Heat, cold, or chemistry do not change how fast a nucleus decays. Radioactivity is a property of the nucleus.
Radioactivity is natural. Rocks, soil, food and even our own bodies contain tiny amounts. Background radiation is always present.

example.q: A sample has 600 decays per second (600 Bq). How many decays happen in 10 seconds, if the rate stays about the same?

analogies.sport: Popcorn in a pan: you cannot tell which kernel will pop next, but you know roughly how many pop each minute.
analogies.nature: Raindrops on a window: each drop is random, but a rainstorm has a steady rate.
analogies.home: Sparkling water fizz: bubbles pop at random.
analogies.city: Cars passing a gate: you cannot predict a single one, but you can count the average per minute.

stages.mnemonic: Unstable nucleus, random decay, steady crowd.

stages.limits: Decay rates are constant under normal conditions. A few rare types of decay change by tiny amounts in extreme conditions.

teach.model: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. They change into more stable ones and give out radiation. This is radioactive decay. It happens randomly for each atom, but in a big group it follows a pattern. It is natural and always around us at low levels.

stages.title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
stages.hook: A sheet of paper, a thin metal plate and a thick concrete wall. Which could stop which kind of radiation?
explain: There are three main kinds of radiation from nuclei. Alpha particles are two protons and two neutrons: a helium nucleus. Beta particles are fast electrons. Gamma rays are waves of energy like very strong light.

They differ in how far they go. Alpha is stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air. Beta goes further and is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Gamma goes furthest, and it takes thick lead or concrete to reduce it a lot.
Alpha is the most ionising: it damages atoms most strongly but over a very short distance. Gamma is the least ionising per distance but the most penetrating.
So an alpha source outside the body is a small risk, but inside the body it is a bigger risk. Gamma sources outside the body need shielding.

example.q: A source's radiation is stopped completely by a sheet of paper. Which kind is it likely to be?
steps: Paper stops only the least penetrating kind.
Beta and gamma pass through paper.

analogies.sport: Alpha is like a heavy shot-put: it hits hard but stops quickly. Gamma is like a light that goes through the window.
analogies.home: Paper stops alpha like a curtain stops sunlight but not a radio signal.
analogies.city: Alpha is stopped by a fence, beta by a wall, gamma needs a bunker.
analogies.tech: Gamma passes through things like a Wi-Fi signal through a wall, but it is far stronger.

misc.right: Alpha is stopped easily, so it matters most when the source gets inside the body. Gamma can go through the body from outside.

stages.limits: Real shielding depends on the energy of the radiation. Neutron radiation is a fourth kind and needs different materials.

stages.title: Half-life
stages.hook: A pile of sweets halves every hour. How long until only one is left from 16?
explain: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time for half of its atoms to decay. After one half-life, half the original atoms remain. After two, a quarter remain. After three, an eighth remain.
Half-lives vary hugely. Some are fractions of a second and some are billions of years. Iodine-131 has a half-life of about 8 days. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5700 years.
A short half-life means a very active but fast-fading source. A long half-life means less activity at any one time but it lasts much longer.
The half-life does not change with temperature or chemistry. It is a property of the isotope.

example.q: A sample has 80 g of an isotope with a half-life of 3 days. How much remains after 9 days?
steps: After 1: 40 g. After 2: 20 g. After 3: 10 g.

analogies.home: A cup of hot tea loses half its remaining extra heat in equal steps, not all at once.
analogies.farm: A trough that is half emptied every hour: 16 litres, 8, 4, 2.
analogies.sport: A knock-out cup: each round half the teams go out.
analogies.music: A note's volume halves each beat: loud, half, quarter.

A nucleus changing and giving out radiation.

misc.wrong: After two half-lives, everything has gone.
misc.right: After two half-lives, a quarter is left. Half of the remaining half decays in the second half-life.

stages.limits: The smooth halving pattern is exact only for very large numbers of atoms. With a few atoms, chance matters.

panel.why: Half-life links activity and time.

teach.model: Half-life is the time for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. After one half-life half is left, after two a quarter, after three an eighth. For example, 80 g with a half-life of 3 days becomes 40 g after 3 days and 20 g after 6 days.

stages.title: Nuclear fission
stages.hook: What if a very heavy atom could split into two pieces and release energy? What would it need to start?
explain: Fission means splitting. In fission, a very heavy nucleus, such as uranium-235, splits into two smaller nuclei. This releases a large amount of energy as heat.
A neutron starts the splitting. When a nucleus splits, it also releases a few more neutrons. These can hit other nuclei and cause them to split too. This is called a chain reaction.
In a power station, the chain reaction is controlled so that, on average, the number of splits stays steady. The heat boils water and makes electricity.
A tiny amount of nuclear fuel releases far more energy than the same mass of coal or oil. But fission also makes radioactive waste that must be handled with great care.

example.q: In a simple chain, each fission causes 2 more fissions. Starting from 1 fission, how many fissions are there in the third step?

analogies.sport: A line of dominoes: one knocks the next. In a reactor, only enough dominoes fall to keep it steady.
analogies.nature: Fallen leaves start a slide of other leaves.
analogies.home: A single match can light a candle which lights others, but we control the flame.
analogies.city: A message passed along a chain of phone calls.

stages.mnemonic: Fission = split, spread neutrons, steady heat.

stages.limits: This is a simple model. Real reactors need careful design for control and safety.

panel.q: Why must a reactor's chain reaction be controlled rather than allowed to grow?
panel.model: If each fission caused more than one more, the rate and heat would keep growing. Control keeps it on average at one new fission per fission so the heat output is steady.
panel.why: Steady output needs balanced neutron numbers.

panel.q: Fission products are often radioactive. What follows from this?
o: Used fuel needs careful storage
It can simply be thrown away with ordinary rubbish
It is safe the moment it leaves the reactor
It is always a gas that blows away
panel.why: Radioactive products need to be managed.

teach.model: In fission, a neutron hits a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 and makes it split. This releases heat and a few more neutrons that can cause more splits. That is a chain reaction. In a reactor it is controlled to give steady heat to make electricity.

stages.title: Nuclear fusion
stages.hook: The Sun has shone for billions of years. What is its fuel, and why is it not burnt out?
explain: Fusion means joining. In fusion, two light nuclei join to make a heavier one and release energy. In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse to make helium.

Nuclei are positive, so they push each other away. To fuse, they need to move extremely fast, which means extremely high temperature, and be squeezed close together. The Sun does this with its huge gravity and about 15 million degrees in its core.

On Earth, scientists are trying to build fusion machines using forms of hydrogen called deuterium and tritium. Fusion produces no long-lived high-level waste of the kind from fission, and its fuel is plentiful.
But fusion is very hard. It has not yet produced steady electricity for the grid. Research continues, and experts disagree about how soon it will be ready.

example.q: In a simple picture, two hydrogen-2 nuclei each have 1 proton. After fusing into one nucleus, how many protons does it have?
steps: A nucleus with 2 protons is helium.

analogies.sport: Two magnets pushing apart: you need a hard shove to bring them together.
analogies.nature: Stars shine because their cores fuse hydrogen into helium.
analogies.home: Like squeezing two sticky balls of clay together to make one bigger ball.
analogies.city: Two crowds forced together through a narrow gate.

stages.mnemonic: Fission splits, fusion fuses: small joins to bigger.
terms: Light nuclei joining to make a heavier nucleus.
A hydrogen isotope with one neutron.
A very hot gas of charged particles.
The very hot, dense centre of a star.

misc.wrong: Fusion power plants already supply electricity.
misc.right: Fusion is still being researched. Experiments have achieved fusion, but not yet routine power for the grid.

stages.limits: Predictions about when fusion power will be ready vary a lot among experts.

trip.prompt: Find the part on stars. Which element do they fuse in their cores?

questions.q: What happens in fusion?
o: Light nuclei join
A heavy nucleus splits
Electrons leave
Water freezes
questions.why: Fusion is joining of nuclei.

questions.q: What does the Sun fuse in its core?
o: Hydrogen into helium
Coal into ash
Helium into iron only
Water into air
questions.why: The Sun's energy comes from hydrogen fusing into helium.

questions.q: Why does fusion need very high temperatures?
o: Nuclei repel each other and must move very fast to get close
Cold makes the nuclei slow and stops them glowing in the core
Nuclei prefer to be hot, so they stick together more easily
The heat is needed to melt the ice and metal around the fuel
questions.why: Positive nuclei repel and need huge speed to overcome it.

questions.q: Two helium-3 nuclei each have 2 protons. How many protons are in the nucleus after joining them?
questions.why: 2 + 2 = 4 protons (which would be beryllium).

questions.q: Match each process with its example.
pairs: Uranium splits in a power station
questions.why: These are three nuclear processes.

questions.q: Which is a challenge for fusion on Earth?
o: Reaching and holding extremely high temperatures
Finding any hydrogen at all on Earth to use as fuel
It cannot make any energy once it has been started
It needs no machines, magnets or heating of any kind
questions.why: Heating and confining plasma is hard.

questions.q: Which statement about fusion is fair?
o: It promises abundant fuel and less long-lived waste, but is not yet a working power source
It is already cheap and used to power most cities today
It has no promise at all and research should be dropped
It is exactly the same process as fission, only with a new name
questions.why: Benefits and challenges both exist.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why fusion is hard to achieve on Earth.
questions.model: Nuclei are positive and repel each other. To make them fuse we need extremely high temperatures and pressure, and we must hold the hot plasma in place long enough.
questions.why: High temperature and confinement are the main challenges.

questions.q: Order from smallest nucleus to largest in a fusion chain.
questions.why: Hydrogen-1 has 1 particle, deuterium has 2, helium-4 has 4.

questions.q: Why does the Sun not have its fusion fuel burn out quickly?
o: It has an enormous amount of hydrogen and fuses it slowly
Fusion in the Sun keeps making new hydrogen as fast as it burns it
The Sun is not really fusing anything and only reflects light
Fusion in the Sun stops each night and restarts each morning
questions.why: It contains vast hydrogen and loses it only gradually over billions of years.

panel.q: Why is fusion described as a possible future energy source but not a current one?
o: Experiments are advancing but steady net electricity has not been shown
It has been banned by most countries after past accidents
There is no hydrogen available on Earth to use as fuel
It was only invented last week and has not yet been tried
panel.why: Research is promising but not yet delivering power to the grid.

panel.q: Compare fission and fusion in one sentence each: what happens to the nuclei?
panel.model: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one.
panel.why: Opposite processes that both release energy under the right conditions.

panel.q: Should we stop funding energy research because the answer is uncertain?
o: Societies weigh uncertain benefits against costs and choose differently
Yes, funding should always stop when the answer is unclear
No, nobody should ever question how money is spent on it
Research has no value for society, even when it is clear
panel.why: Reasonable people disagree about priorities.

teach.model: In fusion, two small nuclei join to make a bigger one and release energy. The Sun does this with hydrogen making helium. It needs extreme heat and pressure because nuclei push each other away. Scientists are trying to make it work on Earth, but it is not ready yet.

points.ask: Do we use it for power now?

stages.title: Nuclear binding energy
stages.hook: A nucleus weighs a little less than its separate parts weigh. Where did the missing mass go?
explain: The particles in a nucleus are held together very strongly. To pull a nucleus completely apart you must add energy. This energy is called the binding energy.
A bound nucleus has slightly less mass than its separate protons and neutrons. This tiny mass difference is turned into energy. Einstein's equation E = mc² links mass and energy.
If we divide the binding energy by the number of particles, we get binding energy per particle. This number is largest for medium-sized nuclei, around iron.
That is why both fission of very heavy nuclei and fusion of very light nuclei can release energy: in both cases, the products are more tightly bound per particle.

example.q: Which nucleus is more tightly bound per particle: one near iron or uranium?
steps: Uranium is on the heavy side, below the peak.
So the iron-region nucleus is more tightly bound per particle.

analogies.sport: A tug of war between two teams that are tied tightly: you need energy to pull them apart.
analogies.home: Magnets stuck together: you must do work to separate them.
analogies.nature: A boulder in a deep hole needs energy to be lifted out.
analogies.tech: A tightly wound spring holds energy.

stages.mnemonic: Tighter bound, less mass, more energy given out when formed.
terms: Energy needed to take a nucleus completely apart.
The small mass lost when particles bind into a nucleus.
Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared.

misc.wrong: Energy is made from nothing in nuclear reactions.
misc.right: A tiny amount of mass changes form into energy. Total mass-energy is conserved.

stages.limits: This is a simple picture. Exact binding energies come from measurements, and the strong force is complex.

trip.prompt: Find the graph of binding energy per nucleon. Where is the peak?

questions.q: What is binding energy?
o: Energy needed to take a nucleus apart
The energy stored in a battery
The energy carried by a beam of light
The energy carried by sound waves
questions.why: It is the energy holding the nucleus together.

questions.q: A nucleus has slightly less mass than its parts. This is the...
o: Mass defect
Mass number
Electron mass
Atomic number
questions.why: That small difference is called the mass defect.

questions.q: What does E = mc² tell us?
o: Mass and energy are linked
Light moves slowly through matter
Mass is always zero in a nucleus
Energy has a colour like paint
questions.why: A small mass equals a very large energy.

questions.q: Near which kind of nucleus is binding energy per particle highest?
o: Medium-sized, around iron
Hydrogen, the lightest nucleus
Uranium, the heaviest natural nucleus
Helium only, and no others
questions.why: The curve peaks near iron.

questions.q: A nucleus has binding energy of 28 MeV and 4 particles. What is the binding energy per particle in MeV?
questions.why: 28 ÷ 4 = 7 MeV per particle.

questions.q: A nucleus has 56 particles and a total binding energy of 492 MeV. What is the binding energy per particle? Round to 1 decimal place.
Why can fusing very light nuclei release energy?
o: The product is more tightly bound per particle
Light nuclei are really very heavy
Fusion needs no energy to get started
The nucleus loses all its protons first
questions.why: Moving up the curve toward iron means energy is released.

questions.q: Why can splitting a very heavy nucleus release energy?
o: The fragments are more tightly bound per particle
Heavy atoms are always very hot
Splitting makes brand new protons
It only moves the electrons around
questions.why: Heavy nuclei are on the far side of the peak, so splitting moves products toward higher binding.

questions.q: Match each idea with its role.
pairs: Missing mass of a bound nucleus
questions.why: These ideas go together.

questions.q: Why can the energy released in a nuclear reaction be very large compared with the mass change?
questions.model: Energy equals mass times c squared, and c squared is an enormous number, so even a tiny mass change corresponds to a lot of energy.
questions.why: The factor c² is huge.

panel.q: A student says energy was created in a reactor. What is a better statement?
o: Some mass changed into energy, and total mass-energy is conserved
Energy came out of nothing at all when the reactor started
Energy was destroyed in the reactor and lost for ever
Mass was simply copied into energy, so there is more of both now
panel.why: Conservation of mass-energy holds.

panel.q: Explain why iron-region nuclei cannot release energy by either fission or fusion.
panel.model: Nuclei near iron have the highest binding energy per particle, so changing them in either direction would move products to lower binding, which would need energy rather than release it.
panel.why: Iron is at the peak of the curve.

panel.q: Why does the Sun end up making heavier elements over a very long time?
o: Fusion builds nuclei toward more tightly bound ones
Gravity turns all the hydrogen straight into iron at once
The Sun cools down, so it stops making any changes at all
Nothing at all ever happens inside the Sun's core
panel.why: In stars, fusion releases energy as nuclei become more tightly bound.

teach.model: Protons and neutrons are held together in a nucleus with binding energy. A bound nucleus has a bit less mass than its parts. That missing mass is turned into energy, as E = mc² says. Nuclei near iron are the most tightly bound per particle.

points.ask: How are mass and energy linked?
Which nuclei are most tightly bound?

stages.title: Nuclear safety fundamentals
stages.hook: A castle has a moat, a wall, a gate and guards. Why have so many layers?
explain: Nuclear safety uses a big idea called defence in depth. This means having several layers of protection, so if one layer fails, the next still protects people.

Layers include good design, strong barriers around the fuel, control systems, backup systems, trained staff and emergency plans. Physical barriers include the fuel itself, the metal fuel covering, the strong reactor vessel and a thick containment building.
People who work with radiation use three basic rules: reduce time, increase distance, and use shielding. Their exposure is measured with personal dosimeters.
A strong safety culture also matters. People are encouraged to report problems and to learn from mistakes, in every country and company.

example.q: A worker must do a job near a source. Which change lowers her radiation dose: halving the time, or doubling the time?
steps: Dose depends on time near the source.
Halving the time halves the dose, if all else is equal.

analogies.city: A road has a speed limit, a guard rail, seat belts and air bags. Many layers.
analogies.sea: A ship has a hull, bulkheads, lifeboats and a crew trained for drills.
analogies.sport: A goalkeeper, defenders and a referee all help prevent trouble.
analogies.home: A house has a smoke alarm, a fire door and an escape plan.

stages.mnemonic: Many layers, each backing up the one before.
terms: A strong building that surrounds the reactor.
A device that records a worker's radiation dose.
A habit of putting safety first and reporting problems.

misc.wrong: One strong wall is enough for safety.
misc.right: Safety rests on several layers, so no single failure can lead to harm.

stages.limits: No technology is risk-free. Safety rules aim to make serious accidents very unlikely and their effects small. Past accidents led to improved designs and rules.

trip.prompt: Find the layers of protection and count how many are listed.

questions.q: What is defence in depth?
o: Several layers of protection
One very thick wall around the plant
Building the plant under the ground only
A special kind of reactor fuel
questions.why: If one layer fails, others still protect.

questions.q: What is a containment building for?
o: To surround the reactor and hold back radioactive material
To store the food and tools for the workers on site
To make the steam that spins the turbine blades
To hold the visitors who come on a school tour
questions.why: It is a strong barrier around the reactor.

questions.q: Which action reduces a worker's dose?
o: Spending less time near the source
Standing much closer to the source
Taking off the shielding in the way
Staying for a longer time near it
questions.why: Dose depends on time, distance and shielding.

questions.q: A worker gets 4 microsieverts of dose per hour at a spot. How many microsieverts will she get in 3 hours?
Another worker at the same spot (4 µSv per hour) works for 30 minutes. What is her dose in µSv?
questions.why: 30 minutes is 0.5 hours: 4 × 0.5 = 2.

questions.q: Match each protection with its idea.
questions.why: Three simple rules.

questions.q: Why does a reactor have backup safety systems?
o: If the main system fails, the backup can still work
To use up more of the electricity that the plant makes
To make the plant louder when it is running at night
Only for decoration inside the control room and building
questions.why: Redundancy is a key part of defence in depth.

questions.q: Why is it a good safety habit for staff to report small problems?
questions.model: Reporting small problems lets them be fixed early, before they become serious, and everyone can learn from them.
questions.why: A strong safety culture catches issues early.

questions.q: Order the barriers from the fuel outward.
questions.why: Each layer surrounds the one before.

questions.q: A worker's badge shows her dose is climbing faster than planned. What should she do?
o: Report it and reduce exposure by leaving or adding protection
Ignore it, since the plan was already made and signed off
Take off the badge so that it stops counting the dose
Work faster near the source so the job is done sooner
questions.why: Dosimeters exist so that action can be taken early.

panel.q: Why are the layers of defence in depth made independent of one another?
o: So one cause cannot defeat them all
To save money on the building work
To make the whole plant more complex
So that none of them can work at all
panel.why: Independence prevents a single fault from disabling every layer.

panel.q: A neighbour says nuclear plants are either perfectly safe or hopelessly dangerous. Give a more balanced view.
panel.model: No technology is risk-free, but nuclear plants use many layers of protection, regulation and trained staff to make serious accidents very unlikely and limit their effects. The risks and benefits should be weighed with evidence.
panel.why: Balanced views avoid extremes.

panel.q: Why is it important to learn from past accidents?
o: To improve designs, rules and training
To forget them as quickly as possible and move on
To find someone to blame for each one, then stop
To stop the making of all electricity from every kind of plant
panel.why: Learning lowers future risk.

teach.model: Nuclear safety uses many layers of protection so that if one fails, the next still works. These include strong barriers around the fuel, backup systems, trained workers and emergency plans. Workers also use time, distance and shielding to limit their dose.
